newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU plans further food safety measures.
newsitem.headline: EU plans further food safety measures.

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday endorsed a call by Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler for tougher measures to protect consumers against mad cow disease, including a ban on exports of British gelatine.

Pressure for extra action has grown following recent EU inspections showing that member states have not been respecting food safety rules to eliminate BSE or bovine spongiform encephalopathy, a deadly brain disease which can be passed from cattle to humans.

"The EU's policy on BSE must continue to evolve in the light of experience and scientific knowledge with the primary objective of reducing the risk to human and animal health to as close to zero as possible," Fischler said in a statement.
Food Safety Commissioner Emma Bonino added that member states were responsible for implementing EU food safety rules.
The Commission is planning to declare British exports of gelatine extracted from British cattle illegal pending new scientific evidence.
But Commission officials said it was only a cosmetic change because Britain has not been exporting locally sourced gelatine.

The EU banned British gelatine exports in March 1996 as part of a world-wide embargo on British beef triggered by London's admission of a link between BSE and its human equivalent, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease.
In June 1996 the European Commission eased the ban on gelatine from British beef, but it has not approved any exports because British manufacturers failed to meet the strict production standards.
Instead they exported gelatine extracted from imported beef.
But the Commission did offer a little joy to British beef exporters with its intention to clarify that beef imported into Britain for processing could be re-exported.
Last November the French government closed the Paris branch of the Hard Rock Cafe, an American-style chain owned by the Rank Organisation, alleging that it had imported frozen hamburger from Britain.
Fischler is also planning to make a fresh attempt to ban specified risk material from cattle and sheep -- brains, eyes, spinal cord and spleen -- from all human and animal food.

In December, EU farm ministers rejected an identical proposal arguing that it was unnecessary and too costly, claiming their countries were virtually free of BSE and scrapie, a similar brain-wasting disease in sheep.

Steps would be taken to ensure that new standards for processing meat and bone meal were respected by all EU member states. Infected meat and bonemeal mixed into cattle and sheep feed is believed to be the main cause of BSE.
The proposed extra measures will be examined by the EU's Standing Veterinary Committee of senior member state officials before the Commission takes a final decision.
